chapterTitle: Everything for Life and Godliness, and the Sure Word
themeTitle: “His Divine Power Has Granted to Us All Things That Pertain to Life and Godliness”

scripture.text: Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have obtained a like precious faith with us in the righteousness of our God and Savior, Jesus Christ:
scripture.understanding: Συμεὼν Πέτρος, “Simon Peter” — many manuscripts spell it Συμεών, the old Hebrew form, Simeon, the name his family used. δοῦλος καὶ ἀπόστολος, “a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” — δοῦλος, from the servant family: wholly owned, like James 1:1; ἀπόστολος, one sent with authority. τοῖς ἰσότιμον ἡμῖν λαχοῦσιν πίστιν, “to those who have obtained a like precious faith with us” — ἰσότιμος, of equal value: the faith of believers who never saw Jesus is as precious as the apostles' own; λαγχάνω, to receive by lot, as a gift, not earned. ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “in the righteousness of our God and Savior, Jesus Christ” — one article governs both nouns, as in Titus 2:13: Jesus is both God and Saviour.

scripture.text: Grace to you and peace be multiplied in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord,
scripture.understanding: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη πληθυνθείη, “Grace to you and peace be multiplied” — the same greeting as 1 Peter 1:2. ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν, “in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord” — ἐπίγνωσις, from the know family: full, personal, experiential knowledge, the relationship that saves, as distinct from γνῶσις (v. 5), knowledge as understanding. Grace and peace grow as knowledge of Christ grows.

scripture.text: seeing that his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue;
scripture.understanding: ὡς πάντα ἡμῖν τῆς θείας δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν δεδωρημένης, “seeing that his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness” — θεῖος, divine; δύναμις, from the power family: God's ability in action; δωρέομαι, from the gift family: to give freely as a gift; ζωή, from the life family; εὐσέβεια, from the godliness family: reverent devotion that shows in life. Nothing needed for spiritual life is missing. διὰ τῆς ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ καλέσαντος ἡμᾶς, “through the knowledge of him who called us” — ἐπίγνωσις again, from the know family. ἰδίᾳ δόξῃ καὶ ἀρετῇ, “by his own glory and virtue” — ἀρετή, excellence, the quality Peter calls believers to add in verse 5.

scripture.text: by which he has granted to us his precious and exceedingly great promises; that through these you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world by lust.
scripture.understanding: δι᾽ ὧν τὰ τίμια καὶ μέγιστα ἡμῖν ἐπαγγέλματα δεδώρηται, “by which he has granted to us his precious and exceedingly great promises” — δωρέομαι again, from the gift family; τίμιος, the ‘precious’ of 1 Peter 1:19; ἐπάγγελμα, a promise. ἵνα διὰ τούτων γένησθε θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως, “that through these you may become partakers of the divine nature” — κοινωνός, a sharer; φύσις, nature. Not becoming God, but sharing His moral character and life by the Spirit. ἀποφυγόντες τῆς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς, “having escaped from the corruption that is in the world by lust” — κόσμος, from the world family; φθορά, decay, rot, which desire brings.

scripture.text: Yes, and for this very cause adding on your part all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge;
scripture.understanding: καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο δὲ σπουδὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες, “Yes, and for this very cause adding on your part all diligence” — σπουδή, earnest effort. God gave everything (v. 3); now you bring everything. ἐπιχορηγήσατε ἐν τῇ πίστει ὑμῶν τὴν ἀρετήν, “in your faith supply moral excellence” — ἐπιχορηγέω, to supply lavishly, from the χορηγός who paid for a chorus; the same verb returns in verse 11. ἀρετή, the ‘virtue’ of verse 3: the WEB uses different English for the same Greek. ἐν δὲ τῇ ἀρετῇ τὴν γνῶσιν, “and in moral excellence, knowledge” — γνῶσις, from the know family: practical understanding, the knowledge that grows, as distinct from ἐπίγνωσις (vv. 2–3), the knowledge that saves.

scripture.text: and in knowledge, self-control; and in self-control perseverance; and in perseverance godliness;
scripture.understanding: ἐν δὲ τῇ γνώσει τὴν ἐγκράτειαν, “and in knowledge, self-control” — γνῶσις, from the know family, then ἐγκράτεια, from the self-control family: mastery of oneself, holding desires in check, as distinct from σωφροσύνη, sound-mindedness. ἐν δὲ τῇ ἐγκρατείᾳ τὴν ὑπομονήν, “and in self-control perseverance” — ὑπομονή, from the endurance family: remaining under a load, the word of James 1:3. ἐν δὲ τῇ ὑπομονῇ τὴν εὐσέβειαν, “and in perseverance godliness” — εὐσέβεια, from the godliness family, as in verse 3. Knowledge without self-control produces the false teachers of chapter 2.

scripture.text: and in godliness brotherly affection; and in brotherly affection, love.
scripture.understanding: ἐν δὲ τῇ εὐσεβείᾳ τὴν φιλαδελφίαν, “and in godliness brotherly affection” — εὐσέβεια, from the godliness family, then φιλαδελφία, from the love family: the warm affection of brothers and sisters. ἐν δὲ τῇ φιλαδελφίᾳ τὴν ἀγάπην, “and in brotherly affection, love” — ἀγάπη, also from the love family: self-giving love that reaches beyond the family to all. The ladder ends where Peter's first letter put both side by side (1 Peter 1:22): φιλαδελφία must grow into ἀγάπη. Love is the crown of all the virtues (Colossians 3:14).

scripture.text: For if these things are yours and abound, they make you to be not idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.
scripture.understanding: ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα καὶ πλεονάζοντα, “For if these things are yours and abound” — πλεονάζω, to increase, to be more and more. οὐκ ἀργοὺς οὐδὲ ἀκάρπους καθίστησιν, “they make you to be not idle or unfruitful” — ἀργός, idle, ‘no-work’, the very word many manuscripts read in James 2:20 for faith without works; ἄκαρπος, fruitless. εἰς τὴν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐπίγνωσιν, “in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ” — ἐπίγνωσις, from the know family: growth in virtue leads into deeper personal knowledge of Christ.

scripture.text: For he who lacks these things is blind, seeing only what is near, having forgotten the cleansing from his old sins.
scripture.understanding: ᾧ γὰρ μὴ πάρεστιν ταῦτα, τυφλός ἐστιν μυωπάζων, “For he who lacks these things is blind, seeing only what is near” — τυφλός, blind; μυωπάζω, to be short-sighted, to squint: he sees only the present and cannot see eternity. λήθην λαβὼν τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ τῶν πάλαι αὐτοῦ ἁμαρτιῶν, “having forgotten the cleansing from his old sins” — λήθη, forgetfulness; καθαρισμός, cleansing, the word Hebrews uses of Christ's work (Hebrews 1:3); ἁμαρτία, from the sin family. Spiritual stagnation begins with forgetting what Christ has done.

scripture.text: Therefore, brothers, be more diligent to make your calling and election sure. For if you do these things, you will never stumble.
scripture.understanding: διὸ μᾶλλον, ἀδελφοί, σπουδάσατε, “Therefore, brothers, be more diligent” — σπουδάζω, the verb of σπουδή (v. 5). βεβαίαν ὑμῶν τὴν κλῆσιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν ποιεῖσθαι, “to make your calling and election sure” — βέβαιος, firm, guaranteed, a legal word for a confirmed title; κλῆσις, God's call; ἐκλογή, His choice. A growing life does not create God's choice; it confirms it in experience. ταῦτα γὰρ ποιοῦντες οὐ μὴ πταίσητέ ποτε, “For if you do these things, you will never stumble” — πταίω, to trip, the word James uses for stumbling in one point of the law and in speech.

scripture.text: For thus you will be richly supplied with the entrance into the eternal Kingdom of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ.
scripture.understanding: οὕτως γὰρ πλουσίως ἐπιχορηγηθήσεται ὑμῖν ἡ εἴσοδος, “For thus you will be richly supplied with the entrance” — ἐπιχορηγέω again, as in verse 5: supply virtue generously, and God will generously supply your welcome. πλουσίως, richly; εἴσοδος, the way in. εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον βασιλείαν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “into the eternal Kingdom of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ” — αἰώνιος, from the time family; σωτήρ, as in verse 1.

scripture.text: Therefore I will not be negligent to remind you of these things, though you know them, and are established in the present truth.
scripture.understanding: διὸ μελλήσω ἀεὶ ὑμᾶς ὑπομιμνῄσκειν περὶ τούτων, “Therefore I will not be negligent to remind you of these things” — ὑπομιμνῄσκω, to remind, the theme of verses 12–15. Believers need reminding more than new information. καίπερ εἰδότας καὶ ἐστηριγμένους ἐν τῇ παρούσῃ ἀληθείᾳ, “though you know them, and are established in the present truth” — εἴδω, from the know family (and the see family); στηρίζω, to make firm, the very word Jesus used: ‘establish your brothers’ (Luke 22:32). Peter is still obeying.

scripture.text: I think it right, as long as I am in this tent, to stir you up by reminding you;
scripture.understanding: δίκαιον δὲ ἡγοῦμαι, “I think it right” — ἡγέομαι, the considered judgement of James 1:2. ἐφ᾽ ὅσον εἰμὶ ἐν τούτῳ τῷ σκηνώματι, “as long as I am in this tent” — σκήνωμα, a tent: the body as a temporary dwelling, the language Paul uses (2 Corinthians 5:1). διεγείρειν ὑμᾶς ἐν ὑπομνήσει, “to stir you up by reminding you” — διεγείρω, to wake fully, the word used of the disciples waking Jesus in the storm.

scripture.text: knowing that the putting off of my tent comes swiftly, even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.
scripture.understanding: εἰδὼς ὅτι ταχινή ἐστιν ἡ ἀπόθεσις τοῦ σκηνώματός μου, “knowing that the putting off of my tent comes swiftly” — εἴδω, from the know family (and the see family): knowing as settled fact; ἀπόθεσις, the ‘putting away’ of 1 Peter 3:21, here taking off the body like a garment or folding a tent; ταχινός, soon, or suddenly. καθὼς καὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐδήλωσέν μοι, “even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me” — δηλόω, to make plain. Jesus had told him by the lake how he would die (John 21:18–19).

scripture.text: Yes, I will make every effort that you may always be able to remember these things even after my departure.
scripture.understanding: σπουδάσω δὲ καὶ ἑκάστοτε ἔχειν ὑμᾶς μετὰ τὴν ἐμὴν ἔξοδον, “Yes, I will make every effort that you may always be able to remember these things even after my departure” — σπουδάζω, as in verse 10; ἔξοδος, ‘exodus’, departure — the very word Moses and Elijah used on the mountain of transfiguration for Jesus' death (Luke 9:31). τὴν τούτων μνήμην ποιεῖσθαι, to keep these things in memory. Early tradition says Mark's Gospel preserved Peter's preaching; this letter is part of his effort.

scripture.text: For we did not follow cunningly devised fables, when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
scripture.understanding: οὐ γὰρ σεσοφισμένοις μύθοις ἐξακολουθήσαντες, “For we did not follow cunningly devised fables” — σοφίζω, to make clever, to contrive; μῦθος, a myth, a made-up story, like the tales of the Greek gods. ἐγνωρίσαμεν ὑμῖν τὴν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ δύναμιν καὶ παρουσίαν, “when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” — δύναμις, from the power family; παρουσία, His royal coming, which the scoffers deny (3:4). ἀλλ᾽ ἐπόπται γενηθέντες τῆς ἐκείνου μεγαλειότητος, “but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty” — ἐπόπτης, from the see family: one who has seen for himself, the noun of ἐποπτεύω (1 Peter 2:12); μεγαλειότης, greatness, splendour.

scripture.text: For he received from God the Father honor and glory, when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
scripture.understanding: λαβὼν γὰρ παρὰ θεοῦ πατρὸς τιμὴν καὶ δόξαν, “For he received from God the Father honor and glory” — τιμή and δόξα. φωνῆς ἐνεχθείσης αὐτῷ τοιᾶσδε ὑπὸ τῆς μεγαλοπρεποῦς δόξης, “when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory” — φέρω, ‘borne’, a word Peter will repeat in verse 21; μεγαλοπρεπής, magnificent, a reverent name for God. “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” — ἀγαπητός, from the love family; εὐδοκέω, to take delight. The same words were heard at Jesus' baptism and on the mountain (Matthew 17:5).

scripture.text: We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.
scripture.understanding: καὶ ταύτην τὴν φωνὴν ἡμεῖς ἠκούσαμεν, “We heard this voice” — ἀκούω: seeing (v. 16) and hearing. ἐξ οὐρανοῦ ἐνεχθεῖσαν, “come out of heaven” — φέρω again. σὺν αὐτῷ ὄντες ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ ὄρει, “when we were with him on the holy mountain” — ὄρος, the mountain, holy because God's presence came there, like Sinai. Peter, James and John were there (Luke 9:28).

scripture.text: We have the more sure word of prophecy; and you do well that you heed it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns, and the morning star arises in your hearts:
scripture.understanding: καὶ ἔχομεν βεβαιότερον τὸν προφητικὸν λόγον, “We have the more sure word of prophecy” — βέβαιος, the ‘sure’ of verse 10; προφητικός, prophetic; λόγος, from the word family. The transfiguration confirmed the prophets; now their word is even more certain. ᾧ καλῶς ποιεῖτε προσέχοντες, “and you do well that you heed it” — καλῶς, from the good family. ὡς λύχνῳ φαίνοντι ἐν αὐχμηρῷ τόπῳ, “as to a lamp shining in a dark place” — φαίνω, from the appear family: to shine; αὐχμηρός, dry, dirty, murky. ἕως οὗ ἡμέρα διαυγάσῃ, “until the day dawns” — ἡμέρα, from the time family. καὶ φωσφόρος ἀνατείλῃ ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, “and the morning star arises in your hearts” — φωσφόρος, ‘light-bearer’, the morning star; Christ calls Himself ‘the Bright and Morning Star’ (Revelation 22:16).

scripture.text: knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation.
scripture.understanding: τοῦτο πρῶτον γινώσκοντες, “knowing this first” — γινώσκω, from the know family: to know by experience and understanding. ὅτι πᾶσα προφητεία γραφῆς ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως οὐ γίνεται, “that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation” — ἐπίλυσις, an untying, an explanation; ἴδιος, one's own. In context (v. 21) the strongest reading is that no prophecy came from the prophet's own interpretation of things; its origin was God. It also implies that Scripture must not be twisted to private meanings (3:16).

scripture.text: For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.
scripture.understanding: οὐ γὰρ θελήματι ἀνθρώπου ἠνέχθη προφητεία ποτέ, “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man” — φέρω, ‘was borne’, the verb of verses 17–18. ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενοι ἐλάλησαν ἀπὸ θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι, “but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit” — φέρω once more: ‘carried along’, as a ship is carried by the wind (Acts 27:15, 17). The voice was borne from heaven; prophecy was not borne by human will; the prophets were borne along by the Spirit. Paul says the same: “Every Scripture is God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16).

visualMeditations.title: The Ladder of Growth
visualMeditations.image: Picture a young vine planted against a wall. The gardener has given it rich soil, sun and water — everything it needs. Year by year it climbs, adding branch upon branch: first a sturdy stem, then side shoots, then leaves, then blossoms, then clusters of grapes. A vine that never climbs, never branches and never fruits is only a stick in the ground.
visualMeditations.meaning: God's power has given us everything for life and godliness (v. 3). Now Peter says, “in your faith supply moral excellence; and in moral excellence, knowledge” (v. 5), “and in knowledge, self-control; and in self-control perseverance; and in perseverance godliness” (v. 6), “and in godliness brotherly affection; and in brotherly affection, love” (v. 7). “For if these things are yours and abound, they make you to be not idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 8). Growth is not optional for a living vine.

visualMeditations.title: The Folded Tent
visualMeditations.image: Picture an old shepherd at dawn, folding his tent for the last time. He has lived in it through many seasons, but now he is moving on to a permanent house. Before he goes, he gathers the younger shepherds around him and tells them again everything he has taught them, so that they will remember after he is gone.
visualMeditations.meaning: “I think it right, as long as I am in this tent, to stir you up by reminding you” (v. 13), “knowing that the putting off of my tent comes swiftly, even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me” (v. 14). Peter writes as a man about to die, and he spends his last effort reminding believers of the truths they already know. What you most need is often not something new, but a fresh grip on what you have already been taught.

visualMeditations.title: Light on the Mountain
visualMeditations.image: Picture three fishermen on a mountain at night, heavy with sleep. Suddenly they wake to see their teacher shining with light brighter than the sun, His clothes dazzling white, and two figures from long ago talking with Him. A bright cloud covers them, and a voice from the cloud says, ‘This is my beloved Son.’ They fall on their faces in terror.
visualMeditations.meaning: “For we did not follow cunningly devised fables, when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (v. 16). “We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain” (v. 18). The Christian faith is not a clever story invented by people. It rests on what real people saw and heard. Peter staked his life — and his death — on it.

visualMeditations.title: The Lamp in the Dark
visualMeditations.image: Picture a traveller in a gloomy, dirty alley at night, holding a small oil lamp. Its circle of light is not large, but it shows him where to step. He keeps walking, guided by the lamp, until the sky behind the rooftops begins to grey, and then the morning star appears, and then the sun rises and floods the whole city with light.
visualMeditations.meaning: “We have the more sure word of prophecy; and you do well that you heed it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns, and the morning star arises in your hearts” (v. 19). Scripture is your lamp in a dark world. It came not from human will, “but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit” (v. 21). Keep walking by its light until the Day dawns and Christ Himself appears.

structure.label: Greeting (v. 1-2)
structure.body: Simon Peter, servant and apostle, writes to those who share an equally precious faith through the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ; may grace and peace be multiplied through the knowledge of God and Jesus.

structure.label: God's Provision and Our Diligence (v. 3-11)
structure.body: God's divine power has given everything needed for life and godliness through knowing Him, and through His promises we share the divine nature, having escaped the world's corruption; so make every effort to add to faith virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection and love; these qualities keep you fruitful, while their absence makes you short-sighted and forgetful; be diligent to confirm your calling and election, and you will receive a rich welcome into Christ's eternal kingdom.

structure.label: Peter's Reminder Before His Death (v. 12-15)
structure.body: Peter will keep reminding them, though they know these truths, because he knows his death is near, as the Lord showed him, and he wants them to remember after his departure.

structure.label: Eyewitnesses and Prophets (v. 16-21)
structure.body: The apostles did not follow clever myths but were eyewitnesses of Christ's majesty on the holy mountain, where they heard the Father's voice; the prophetic word is made more certain, a lamp in a dark place until the day dawns; no prophecy came from human will, but people spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: Everything You Need, and Everything You Must Add
paragraphs: Peter opens with a staggering claim: “seeing that his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue” (v. 3). Believers are not spiritual beggars waiting for some missing ingredient. In knowing Christ they already have every resource for spiritual life and godly living. And through God's “precious and exceedingly great promises” (v. 4) they share the divine nature — not becoming God, but receiving His life and reflecting His character by the Spirit, having escaped the corruption that desire produces.

But God's provision does not make us passive. “Yes, and for this very cause adding on your part all diligence” (v. 5). Because God has given everything, we must give everything. Peter then lists eight qualities in a chain, each growing out of the one before: faith, moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection and love. Faith is the root; love is the crown. Paul's fruit of the Spirit makes the same point: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith” (Galatians 5:22).

Two warnings follow. Growth produces fruit: “For if these things are yours and abound, they make you to be not idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 8). Its absence produces blindness: “For he who lacks these things is blind, seeing only what is near, having forgotten the cleansing from his old sins” (v. 9). A Christian who stops growing becomes short-sighted — fixed on the present, unable to see eternity — and forgetful of the grace that saved him. That is exactly the kind of person false teachers find easy to deceive.

sections.heading: Making Your Calling Sure
paragraphs: “Therefore, brothers, be more diligent to make your calling and election sure. For if you do these things, you will never stumble” (v. 10). Peter does not mean that our efforts create God's choice of us — He called us “by his own glory and virtue” (v. 3). He means that a growing, fruitful life confirms that the call was real, both to ourselves and to others. James said the same about faith and works. Assurance grows as godliness grows.

The reward is a generous welcome: “For thus you will be richly supplied with the entrance into the eternal Kingdom of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ” (v. 11). The same verb — ἐπιχορηγέω, to supply lavishly — is used in verse 5 and verse 11. Supply virtue generously, and God will supply your entrance generously. Some will be saved ‘as through fire’; Peter wants his readers to enter the kingdom with a rich welcome.

Then Peter explains why he keeps repeating himself: he is about to die. “knowing that the putting off of my tent comes swiftly, even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me” (v. 14). Jesus had told him: “But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you, and carry you where you don’t want to go” (John 21:18). Peter calls his death his ‘exodus’ (v. 15), the same word used of Jesus' death on the mountain of transfiguration: Moses and Elijah “spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). Peter goes to his own departure following his Lord.

sections.heading: Not Fables, but Eyewitnesses and Prophets
paragraphs: False teachers apparently claimed that the apostles' message — especially about Christ's power and return — was a myth. Peter answers with testimony: “For we did not follow cunningly devised fables, when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (v. 16). On the mountain he saw Christ's glory and heard the Father's voice: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (v. 17). The transfiguration was a preview of the coming kingdom. John says the same: “We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

Then Peter points beyond his own experience to Scripture: “We have the more sure word of prophecy; and you do well that you heed it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns, and the morning star arises in your hearts” (v. 19). The transfiguration confirmed what the prophets had said. Their word is a lamp in a murky world, enough to walk by until Christ returns and fills the heart with full light.

Finally, Peter explains why Scripture is trustworthy: “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit” (v. 21). The prophets were real people who spoke real words, but they were ‘carried along’ by the Spirit like a ship by the wind. Paul says, “Every Scripture is God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16). That is why Scripture must not be bent to private interpretations (v. 20), and why it is the believer's final defence against false teaching (chapter 2).

ntConnection.heading: The Transfiguration Remembered
paragraphs: The Gospels record the event Peter remembers. Jesus “took with him Peter, John, and James, and went up onto the mountain to pray” (Luke 9:28). Moses and Elijah “appeared in glory, and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). “Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they were fully awake, they saw his glory” (Luke 9:32). And “A voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son. Listen to him!’” (Luke 9:35). Matthew records the words Peter quotes: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him” (Matthew 17:5).

On the mountain Peter had wanted to build three shelters — tents — to keep the moment. Now, years later, he speaks of his own body as a tent about to be folded (vv. 13–14), and of his death as an exodus. Paul uses the same picture: “For we know that if the earthly house of our tent is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal, in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

The morning star of verse 19 shines at the end of the Bible: “I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you for the assemblies. I am the root and the offspring of David; the Bright and Morning Star” (Revelation 22:16). And the ladder of virtues finds its summit where Paul places it too: “But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13).

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment, acknowledgement.” ἐπίγνωσις is the key word of 2 Peter. It is the personal, relational knowledge of God and Christ that saves and transforms (vv. 2, 3, 8). γνῶσις (vv. 5–6) is understanding that grows as part of the Christian life. Both are in the know family. The false teachers had a kind of knowledge, but not ἐπίγνωσις that produces godliness. Peter's last words are ‘grow in the grace and knowledge’ (3:18).

Strong's: “to furnish besides, i.e. fully supply, (figuratively) aid or contribute.” The word comes from the χορηγός, the wealthy citizen who paid all the costs of a chorus at a Greek festival — and did it lavishly. Peter uses it twice: believers are to supply virtue to their faith generously (v. 5), and God will supply their entrance into the kingdom generously (v. 11). Peter used the simpler χορηγέω in 1 Peter 4:11 for the strength God supplies. Generosity in growth meets generosity in welcome.

Strong's: “self-control (especially continence).” ἐγκράτεια means mastery over oneself — holding power over one's own desires. It belongs to the self-control family, alongside σωφροσύνη (sound-mindedness) and νήφω (sobriety). Paul lists it as part of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23). In 2 Peter it stands in sharp contrast to the false teachers of chapter 2, who promise freedom while being slaves to their desires. True knowledge produces self-control; false knowledge excuses its absence.

Strong's: “an exit, i.e. (figuratively) death.” ἔξοδος is the word from which ‘exodus’ comes. It is used of Israel's departure from Egypt (Hebrews 11:22) and of Jesus' death in Luke 9:31, spoken of by Moses and Elijah on the mountain. Peter uses it of his own death. For the believer, death is not an ending but an exodus — a departure from slavery and a journey home. Peter pairs it with σκήνωμα, a tent: the body is a temporary dwelling, folded up when the journey moves on.

Strong's: “to "bear" or carry (in a very wide application, literally and figuratively, as follows)”. Peter uses φέρω four times: the voice was ‘borne’ to Christ (v. 17) and ‘borne’ from heaven (v. 18); prophecy was never ‘borne’ by human will, but men spoke as they were ‘borne along’ by the Holy Spirit (v. 21). Luke uses it of a ship driven by the wind (Acts 27:15, 17). The prophets were not passive, but the Spirit was the wind in their sails. That is why their word is sure.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this chapter the Holy Spirit reminds you of what you already have, calls you to grow, and anchors you in a word you can trust.

items.title: You Are Not Lacking
items.body: Do you feel that you need some special experience or secret before you can live a godly life? The Spirit says you already have “all things that pertain to life and godliness” (v. 3) in knowing Christ. What you need is not more supply but more diligence. Which of the qualities in verses 5–7 is He asking you to add right now?

items.title: Have You Become Short-Sighted?
items.body: Peter warns of believers who are “blind, seeing only what is near, having forgotten the cleansing from his old sins” (v. 9). Are you so focused on today's problems and pleasures that you have lost sight of eternity? Have you forgotten how much you were forgiven? Ask the Spirit to clear your vision and remind you of the cross.

items.title: Is the Lamp Lit?
items.body: God has given you a lamp for the dark places — His word (v. 19). Are you walking by it, or stumbling in the dark? The Spirit who carried the prophets along wants to speak to you through what they wrote. Commit to heeding it daily until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your heart.

audit.title: The Growth Check
audit.body: Look at the list in verses 5–7. Which quality is strongest in you? Which is weakest? What is one step you can take to add the weakest one this month?

audit.title: The Memory Check
audit.body: When did you last thank God specifically for the cleansing of your old sins (v. 9)? Have you grown proud, cold or careless because you have forgotten?

audit.title: The Word Check
audit.body: Is Scripture your lamp, or only a decoration (v. 19)? Which voices — teachers, influencers, opinions — are you trusting more than God's word?

practices.title: Eight Weeks Up the Ladder
practices.body: For the next eight weeks, focus on one quality from verses 5–7 each week: faith, moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, love. Each Monday, read the verse, find one other Scripture about that quality, and choose one practical way to practise it that week. Review at the end of each week.

practices.title: Leave a Reminder
practices.body: Peter wanted believers to remember after his departure (v. 15). Write a letter to someone younger in the faith — a child, a new believer, a friend — reminding them of the core truths of the gospel and the things you most want them to remember about following Jesus. Give it to them, or keep it to give at the right time.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, our God and Saviour, thank You for giving me a faith as precious as the apostles' own. Multiply grace and peace to me as I grow in knowing You. Thank You that Your divine power has given me everything I need for life and godliness, and that through Your precious and very great promises I share in Your nature and escape the corruption of the world. Make me diligent. Add to my faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge self-control, to self-control perseverance, to perseverance godliness, to godliness brotherly affection, and to brotherly affection love. Keep me from being idle or fruitless. Open my eyes where I have become short-sighted, and never let me forget that You cleansed me from my old sins. Confirm my calling and election in the way I live, and grant me a rich welcome into Your eternal kingdom. Thank You for eyewitnesses who saw Your majesty and heard the Father's voice, and for the prophetic word, spoken by men carried along by the Holy Spirit. Let Your word be my lamp in every dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in my heart. When the time comes for my own tent to be folded, let my departure be an exodus home to You. In Your name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: The Transfiguration
storyConnections.summary: Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain to pray. As He prayed, His face shone like the sun and His clothes became dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appeared, speaking with Him about the departure He would accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter, half-awake and terrified, offered to build three shelters. Then a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him” (Matthew 17:5). The disciples fell on their faces until Jesus touched them. Decades later Peter writes that this was no myth: he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty.

storyConnections.title: Jesus Foretells Peter's Death
storyConnections.summary: After restoring Peter by the lake, Jesus said to him, “But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you, and carry you where you don’t want to go” (John 21:18). “Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, ‘Follow me’” (John 21:19). Peter carried that word for more than thirty years. In 2 Peter he writes that the putting off of his tent is coming soon, ‘even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me’. Church tradition says he was crucified in Rome under Nero.

storyConnections.title: Paul's Ship Driven by the Wind
storyConnections.summary: On his voyage to Rome as a prisoner, Paul's ship was caught by a violent north-easterly wind. The sailors could not steer against it, “we gave way to it, and were driven along” (Acts 27:15). Luke uses the same verb, φέρω, that Peter uses for the prophets ‘carried along’ by the Holy Spirit. The ship was real, its crew was real, its timbers creaked — but its course was set by a power beyond them. So with the prophets: real men, real words, but carried along by the Spirit to speak from God.
